```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(here)
library(tidyverse)

here::i_am("errata.qmd")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

out <- function(file) {
  read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", file), show_col_types = FALSE)
}

one_dp <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
two_dp <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)

# Entry 1: the two study rows of table 2.2, whose labels are interchanged.
table_2.2 <- out("table_2.2_lrl_reanalysis.csv")
lrl_cell <- function(content_label, panel, group) {
  row <- table_2.2 |>
    filter(content_factor == content_label, outcome_variable == panel)
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1)
  one_dp(row[[paste("Capital Punishment", group)]])
}
pro_study <- function(panel, group) lrl_cell("After pro capital punishment study", panel, group)
anti_study <- function(panel, group) lrl_cell("After anti capital punishment study", panel, group)

# Entry 2: chapter 6's prose against the chapter 6 tables it describes. The corrected
# figures are the book's own printed cells, read from the transcription rather than from a
# run, because the estimator behind them has no seed.
published_maintext <- read_csv(here::here("ground_truth", "published_maintext_tables.csv"),
                               show_col_types = FALSE)
seed_dispersion <- read_csv(here::here("ground_truth", "seed_dispersion.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)
printed_pct <- function(float, panel_label, row) {
  cell <- published_maintext |>
    filter(table == float, panel == panel_label, row_label == row)
  stopifnot(nrow(cell) == 1)
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * as.numeric(cell$value_paper))
}
c6 <- tribble(
  ~float,      ~panel,     ~row_label,                       ~quantity,                        ~in_prose,
  "table_6.2", "estimate", "Prediction: weaker persistence", "Prediction: weaker persistence", 0.20,
  "table_6.3", "10 days",  "Overall",                        "Overall, 10 days",               0.46,
  "table_6.3", "30 days",  "Overall",                        "Overall, 30 days",               0.44,
  "table_6.3", "10 days",  "Republican",                     "Republican, 10 days",            0.57,
  "table_6.3", "10 days",  "Democrat",                       "Democrat, 10 days",              0.43
) |>
  left_join(published_maintext |> select(float = table, panel, row_label, in_table = value_paper),
            by = c("float", "panel", "row_label")) |>
  left_join(seed_dispersion, by = c("float", "quantity")) |>
  mutate(table_inside = in_table >= minimum - 1e-9 & in_table <= maximum + 1e-9,
         prose_inside = in_prose >= minimum - 1e-9 & in_prose <= maximum + 1e-9)
stopifnot(nrow(c6) == 5, !any(is.na(c6$in_table)), !any(is.na(c6$minimum)),
          all(c6$table_inside), !any(c6$prose_inside), n_distinct(c6$n_seeds) == 1)
c6_seeds <- unique(c6$n_seeds)

# Entry 3: the Hiscox expert cue persistence estimates.
table_6.4 <- out("table_6.4_all_persistence.csv")
hiscox <- function(sample_label) {
  row <- table_6.4 |>
    filter(str_starts(study_label, "Hiscox"), Sample == sample_label,
           Treatment == "Expert cue")
  stopifnot(nrow(row) == 1)
  100 * as.numeric(str_extract(row$`Persistence Ratio`, "^[-0-9.]+"))
}
hiscox_mturk <- round(hiscox("MTurk"))
hiscox_gfk <- round(hiscox("GfK"))

# Entry 4: the convincingness ratings in the lower half of table 2.3.
convincing <-
  out("table_2.3_gc_replication.csv") |>
  filter(rating == "convincing", str_detect(predisposition, "Proponents"))
stopifnot(nrow(convincing) == 1)

# Entry 5: the standard error of the two-sided effect on support among opponents.
two_sided_se <-
  out("figure_5.17_gc_pro_con_effects.csv") |>
  filter(dv == "support_recode_change", term == "Pro Con",
         predisposition == "Capital Punishment Opponents")
stopifnot(nrow(two_sided_se) == 1)
```

Five errata in *Persuasion in Parallel: How Information Changes Minds about Politics*
(University of Chicago Press, 2022), <https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226821832.001.0001>.
None of the five changes any conclusion the book draws. Every corrected value below is
computed at render time rather than typed: four of the five from the maintained reanalysis in
`active-maintenance-aec/coppock_2022`, and entry 2 from the book's own printed tables, held in
that repository's transcription of them.

**Provenance.** Every discrepancy below was checked against the printed edition. The
reanalysis itself reads an uncorrected proof dated 26 May 2022, so each quoted sentence was
verified against the published book rather than taken from that file. These are properties of
the book as printed, not of any one rendering of it.

---

**1.** In table 2.2 (p. 26), the two study rows carry each other's labels, in both panels.

> Change in attitudes toward the death penalty
>
> | | Proponents | Opponents |
> |---|---|---|
> | After **pro**-capital punishment study | `r anti_study("attitude", "Proponents")` | `r anti_study("attitude", "Opponents")` |
> | After **anti**-capital punishment study | `r pro_study("attitude", "Proponents")` | `r pro_study("attitude", "Opponents")` |
>
> Change in beliefs in deterrent efficacy
>
> | | Proponents | Opponents |
> |---|---|---|
> | After **pro**-capital punishment study | `r anti_study("belief", "Proponents")` | `r anti_study("belief", "Opponents")` |
> | After **anti**-capital punishment study | `r pro_study("belief", "Proponents")` | `r pro_study("belief", "Opponents")` |

*Corrected:*

> Change in attitudes toward the death penalty
>
> | | Proponents | Opponents |
> |---|---|---|
> | After **anti**-capital punishment study | `r anti_study("attitude", "Proponents")` | `r anti_study("attitude", "Opponents")` |
> | After **pro**-capital punishment study | `r pro_study("attitude", "Proponents")` | `r pro_study("attitude", "Opponents")` |
>
> Change in beliefs in deterrent efficacy
>
> | | Proponents | Opponents |
> |---|---|---|
> | After **anti**-capital punishment study | `r anti_study("belief", "Proponents")` | `r anti_study("belief", "Opponents")` |
> | After **pro**-capital punishment study | `r pro_study("belief", "Proponents")` | `r pro_study("belief", "Opponents")` |

The changed artifact is the two labels alone. Every value is correct, and the rows are in
the order the analysis produces them, whose study-content factor runs con before pro and so
puts the anti-capital punishment study first. Figure 2.2, printed on the same page from the
same variable, shows the con study at `r anti_study("attitude", "Proponents")` for
proponents and `r anti_study("attitude", "Opponents")` for opponents and the pro study at
`r pro_study("attitude", "Proponents")` and `r pro_study("attitude", "Opponents")`, which is
the table's two rows the other way up. The sentence beneath the figure, reporting that
self-assessed change is higher in the pro condition than in the null and higher in the null
than in the con, says the same thing again. The "Combined" rows are sums of the two and are
unaffected, as is the reading of the table that the surrounding text draws from them.

---

**2.** Four sentences in chapter 6 report persistence figures that the chapter's own tables
print differently.

Every persistence figure in chapter 6 comes from a bootstrap the deposited code runs without
a seed, so no rerun can settle what these sentences should say. The tables can, and each
corrected figure below is the number the book's own table 6.2 or table 6.3 prints for the same
quantity. The tables are also the side the estimator supports: run at `r c6_seeds` seeds, all
five of the figures the tables print fall inside the range their quantity takes across seeds,
and none of the five figures the prose gives does.

*Page 114.*

> Across all 12 studies, the average persistence ratio was about one-third, or 34 percent;
> that figure is 50 percent in the stronger persistence group and **20** percent in the
> weaker persistence group (see table 6.2).

*Corrected:*

> Across all 12 studies, the average persistence ratio was about one-third, or 34 percent;
> that figure is 50 percent in the stronger persistence group and
> **`r printed_pct("table_6.2", "estimate", "Prediction: weaker persistence")`** percent in
> the weaker persistence group (see table 6.2).

*Page 117.*

> After ten days treatment effects decay to **46** percent (SE = 5 percent) of their original
> magnitudes.

*Corrected:*

> After ten days treatment effects decay to
> **`r printed_pct("table_6.3", "10 days", "Overall")`** percent (SE = 5 percent) of their
> original magnitudes.

> After thirty days, average persistence declines to **44** percent (SE = 6 percent).

*Corrected:*

> After thirty days, average persistence declines to
> **`r printed_pct("table_6.3", "30 days", "Overall")`** percent (SE = 6 percent).

*Page 118.*

> For Republicans, persistence after ten days averaged **57** percent; this figure was **43**
> percent for Democrats.

*Corrected:*

> For Republicans, persistence after ten days averaged
> **`r printed_pct("table_6.3", "10 days", "Republican")`** percent; this figure was
> **`r printed_pct("table_6.3", "10 days", "Democrat")`** percent for Democrats.

The page 118 sentence is the one that moves furthest, and the two halves fail differently. Its
57 percent is table 6.3's Republican estimate after *thirty* days, read one column across from
the ten-day estimate the sentence describes; its 43 percent is no cell of the table at all. The
sentence that follows, that the Republican and Democratic estimates are not statistically
significantly different, is unaffected and holds on the corrected figures, which are closer
together than the published pair. The standard errors on page 117 are left as printed. The
ten-day one agrees with table 6.3; the thirty-day one says 6 percent where the table prints
0.05, but the reanalysis returns 6 percent as well, so that figure sits inside the bootstrap's
noise in a way none of the five estimates above does. Tables 6.2 and 6.3 are otherwise correct
as printed and are not reprinted here.

---

**3.** Page 114 attributes a persistence estimate to a sample that is not in the
persistence analysis.

> Curiously, the different replications of the Hiscox (2006) "expert" treatment generated
> very different persistence estimates: `r hiscox_mturk` percent on MTurk but
> `r hiscox_gfk` percent on **Lucid**.

*Corrected:*

> Curiously, the different replications of the Hiscox (2006) "expert" treatment generated
> very different persistence estimates: `r hiscox_mturk` percent on MTurk but
> `r hiscox_gfk` percent on **GfK**.

Table 6.1 lists twelve panel survey experiments and none of them is fielded on Lucid; the
Hiscox rows of table 6.4 are Mechanical Turk and GfK, and table 6.4 gives the zero to GfK.
The two percentages are left at the whole numbers the sentence uses because they come from
a bootstrap the analysis runs without a seed, and a decimal place would state a precision
the estimator does not have.

---

**4.** In the lower half of table 2.3, the difference between the two convincingness
ratings for proponents does not equal the difference between the two cells printed above
it.

The table prints `r one_dp(convincing$pro_study)` for the pro-capital punishment study and
`r one_dp(convincing$anti_study)` for the anti-capital punishment study, and gives their
difference as **3.0**. The difference is **`r one_dp(convincing$difference)`**. The changed
artifact is that single cell; every other cell in both halves of the table reproduces.

---

**5.** Page 101 gives a standard error that disagrees with the book's own appendix
table A.5.

> As shown in the left facet, the average effect of the two-sided message on support for
> capital punishment is very close to zero for both proponents (0.28 scale points, SE:
> 0.18) and opponents (0.10, SE: **0.11**).

*Corrected:*

> As shown in the left facet, the average effect of the two-sided message on support for
> capital punishment is very close to zero for both proponents (0.28 scale points, SE:
> 0.18) and opponents (0.10, SE: **`r two_dp(two_sided_se$std.error)`**).

Table A.5 reports `r two_dp(two_sided_se$std.error)` for this same standard error, and the
reanalysis reproduces the appendix. The other seven quantities in the passage are correct
as printed.
